strengths: The paper addresses a compelling and relatively underexplored problem: transferring a temporally evolving effect from an example video while preserving the target video's content and motion. This is meaningfully different from conventional text-guided editing or static-reference conditioning and is potentially useful for practical video creation.

RefVFX is feed-forward at inference time and supports both image-to-video and video-to-video settings. The construction of training triplets from two examples sharing an effect is sensible, and jointly conditioning a strong video backbone on the target and reference videos is technically plausible.

The multi-source dataset is substantial, with more than 120K triplets and complementary LoRA-based, neural video-to-video, and programmatic effects. The automated neural-pair pipeline and controllable programmatic pipeline are valuable engineering contributions that could facilitate subsequent work if fully released.

The experiments cover held-out LoRA effects, novel neural-effect prompts, programmatic effects, several text-conditioned baselines, quantitative embeddings, user preferences, and qualitative examples. Reported reference-adherence preferences are large: approximately 75–82% for I2V, 78–94% for neural V2V, and 94–98% for code-based effects.

The qualitative examples show capabilities not readily available from prompt-only baselines, including transferring ordered transformations, interactions, camera behavior, and spatially varying temporal effects. The independent guidance controls for target preservation and effect strength are also practically useful.

The presentation is generally clear, with helpful diagrams of the data-generation pipelines and conditioning architecture. The limitations section appropriately identifies failures on occlusion and interaction, human-centric data bias, and the roughly doubled inference cost.
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not provide sufficiently controlled evidence that the model transfers an effect independently of reference content. VideoPrism similarity between output and reference can reward copying semantic content, identity, scene, or motion rather than the intended effect; first-frame similarity likewise does not adequately measure preservation of the complete input video. No effect-specific temporal metric or disentanglement test is presented.

Although the data-generation pipelines naturally produce paired edited targets, the evaluation is described as lacking ground-truth triplets. Consequently, there is no direct comparison against the intended output, even for synthetic effects where exact targets and masks should be available. This is a major missed opportunity to measure effect timing, spatial application, and target-motion preservation objectively.

The baseline comparison is intrinsically asymmetric: RefVFX receives the full reference video plus text, whereas all external baselines receive only a textual description. These comparisons establish that reference conditioning is useful, but they do not isolate the quality of the proposed architecture from the additional information supplied. The only reference-related ablation is removal of the reference; alternative reference encoders, attention mechanisms, retrieval/copying controls, and parameter-matched reference-conditioned baselines are absent.

The user study is underreported. The paper gives numbers of valid annotations but not the number or expertise of raters, number and sampling of evaluated videos, assignments per pair, randomization and blinding procedures, quality-control criteria, aggregation protocol, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The supplement promises further study details but does not provide them. Thus, the impressive win rates are difficult to audit.

Evidence for broad generalization is limited. Code-based testing uses the same operation and transition families as training and changes only sampled hyperparameters; neural V2V validation is produced by the same synthetic pipeline and generator family; and the dataset is strongly human-centric. These settings do not fully support broad claims about arbitrary unseen temporal-effect categories or real-world videos.

The claimed 1,700-effect diversity is potentially misleading because roughly 1,500 entries arise from combinations and parameterizations of a comparatively small library of programmatic operations and transitions. Dataset counts should distinguish semantic effect classes, operator combinations, and parameter instances, and performance should be broken down by genuinely novel families.

Important ablations are missing: contributions of each of the three data sources, cross-source transfer, the text condition, target last-frame conditioning during training, reference/input dropout, token concatenation choices, training-set scale, and reference–target content similarity. These are necessary to understand why the system works and whether it learns transferable temporal structure rather than artifacts of its synthetic pipelines.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated release intention. LoRA rank, optimizer, learning rate, schedule, dropout probabilities, guidance weights, detailed sampling proportions, exact neural-effect prompts, filtering criteria, and user-study protocol are absent. The open-source LoRAs are named but their individual provenance and licenses are not clearly documented, which also raises redistribution and attribution questions for the proposed dataset.

The conditioning design is a relatively direct extension of the Wan/VACE latent-concatenation mechanism. Given this modest algorithmic novelty, the paper's case depends heavily on the dataset and empirical validation; the evaluation and reporting gaps therefore tip the balance slightly toward rejection, despite the promising task and qualitative results.

strengths: The reference-video-conditioned temporal-effect-transfer task is interesting and relevant to computer vision; using a video example can express dynamics that are difficult to specify through text or static keyframes.

The paper assembles a sizeable, diverse training collection—over 120K triplets and 1,700 effects—from LoRA-generated, neural V2V, and programmatic sources. The construction strategy of pairing two independently generated instances of the same effect is sensible for discouraging direct content copying.

RefVFX supports both image-to-video and video-to-video transfer in a feed-forward model, and its classifier-free guidance formulation provides useful control over input preservation versus reference adherence.

The qualitative examples are promising, and the reported human preferences consistently favor RefVFX over the tested prompt-based systems. The limitations section also candidly identifies failures involving occlusion, interaction, domain coverage, and computational cost. weaknesses: The central evaluation does not convincingly measure effect transfer. VideoPrism similarity between the output and the entire reference video conflates the desired temporal effect with appearance, objects, scene content, and motion. Likewise, similarity to the input cannot distinguish faithful preservation from under-editing. No ground-truth outputs or effect-specific temporal measurements are used.

The baseline comparison is structurally weak: all principal competitors are prompt-only and cannot observe the reference video. Their inferior reference adherence is therefore largely expected. A convincing evaluation needs reference-conditioned alternatives or well-designed adaptations, simple latent/token concatenation baselines, shuffled or mismatched-reference controls, and ablations of the proposed conditioning design and each training-data source.

Claims of generalization to unseen effect categories are overstated. Neural V2V validation data are created and manually filtered using the same pipeline as training; code-based tests reuse the same operation and transition families with only new hyperparameters; and the manuscript does not establish that held-out LoRAs are semantically disjoint from training effects. Evaluation on diverse, independently sourced real reference videos is largely absent.

The human study is insufficiently documented to serve as the main evidence. The paper reports numbers of annotations but not the number of raters and unique test cases, sampling and aggregation procedures, rater recruitment, blinding, randomization, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The relationship between the reported win rates and mean scores is also unclear, especially for the no-reference ablation.

The method is technically incremental: it fine-tunes an existing Wan model with LoRA and introduces additional conditioning through latent concatenation. The manuscript provides no controlled architectural ablation showing that this particular design is preferable to straightforward alternatives. The more distinctive contribution is the dataset, making Datasets/Benchmarks arguably the more appropriate contribution type, but the benchmark evidence and release specification are not mature enough to support acceptance under that framing either.

Reproducibility is poor. Important details such as LoRA rank, optimizer, learning rate and schedule, exact conditioning-drop probabilities, dataset mixture sizes, prompt construction, filtering criteria, and key architectural settings are missing despite the text claiming that the supplement provides them. Code and data are only promised after publication, and the main paper contains a placeholder website URL.

The dataset provenance needs substantially better documentation. Individual community LoRAs, their licenses and permissions, deduplication procedures, source-data licensing, filtering rates, and safeguards against identity misuse are not adequately addressed. This is especially important for a model capable of transferring person-centric transformations.

The evidence therefore does not support broad claims of faithful, category-level temporal-effect disentanglement. The paper shows a promising system and data-generation direction, but consequential evaluation, comparison, and reproducibility gaps currently favor rejection.

strengths: The paper introduces a compelling and practically useful problem: feed-forward transfer of time-varying visual effects from a reference video to a target image or video. This is meaningfully different from conventional text-guided editing and static-reference personalization.

The multi-source data construction is a substantial contribution. Combining LoRA-derived effects, a scalable neural V2V pair-generation pipeline, and controllable programmatic effects yields over 120K triplets spanning more than 1,700 effects.

The proposed conditioning mechanism is conceptually simple and compatible with a strong video-diffusion backbone. Jointly conditioning on the input video, reference video, and text also supports useful independent guidance controls for input preservation and effect strength.

The qualitative examples are persuasive: RefVFX captures temporally evolving transformations that prompt-only baselines frequently omit, while generally retaining target content and motion. The reported human preferences are large and consistently favor the method in reference adherence.

Evaluation covers I2V, neural V2V, and code-based effects, includes unseen effect instances, multiple contemporary baselines, an ablation without reference conditioning, perceptual metrics, and an explicit discussion of failure cases and computational cost.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not include ground-truth transferred videos. VideoPrism similarity to the entire reference is an ambiguous proxy because it can reward copying reference content, identity, or scene appearance rather than isolating the intended effect. Likewise, input similarity rewards under-editing. The reported numerical improvements are often modest and lack uncertainty estimates.

The human study is central to the scientific case, but essential protocol details are missing: the number and demographics of participants, number of evaluated examples, sampling and assignment procedure, interface, randomization/blinding, quality control, inter-rater agreement, per-comparison sample counts, confidence intervals, and significance tests. Raw annotation counts alone are insufficient to establish statistical reliability.

The baselines are all prompt-conditioned and cannot consume the reference video, making the strong reference-adherence advantage partly expected. Comparisons to stronger adaptations that extract dense captions, motion trajectories, or reference embeddings—or that receive matched computational/training resources—would better establish the benefit of the particular architecture and dataset.

Generalization is not yet demonstrated broadly enough. Much of the validation is generated using the same LoRA ecosystem or the same neural/programmatic pipelines as training, with only effects, prompts, or hyperparameters held out. Evaluation on independently collected real reference videos and out-of-domain targets would be substantially more convincing.

Important ablations are absent, including the contributions of each data source, reference-conditioning design, text conditioning, dataset scale, and training mixture. It is therefore unclear which components drive performance or whether simpler conditioning alternatives would work comparably well.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the promised code release: LoRA rank, optimizer, learning rate, conditioning-dropout probabilities, dataset split sizes, exact V2V data quantity, filtering criteria, and many inference/guidance settings are unspecified. The claim that the dataset establishes a benchmark is also premature without a clearly defined public release, fixed test protocol, and ground truth.

The method doubles latent token count and takes roughly seven minutes for a 33-frame, 480p clip on an A100. Together with the human-centric training distribution and documented failures on occlusion and complex interactions, this limits current applicability. Data licensing, consent, misuse risks, and the provenance of downloaded LoRAs also deserve discussion.

strengths: The paper identifies a compelling and underexplored task: transferring time-varying effects from a reference video while preserving a target video's content and motion. This is more expressive than prompt-only or static-reference editing.

RefVFX combines a practical conditioning design with a substantial data contribution: over 120K triplets spanning LoRA-derived, neural video-to-video, and reproducible programmatic effects. The three sources provide useful complementary coverage.

Evaluation includes unseen effects, image-to-video and video-to-video settings, qualitative comparisons, embedding metrics, and a relatively large human study with over 15,000 annotations from more than 500 annotators.

The comparison with the No-Ref ablation is informative: human preferences favor full reference conditioning, especially for overall match, providing evidence that the reference video contributes beyond the text and input video.

The paper is generally clear, figures communicate the task effectively, and limitations such as occlusion failures, human-centric data bias, and approximately doubled inference cost are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: The primary baseline comparison is intrinsically asymmetric: RefVFX receives the reference video in addition to the detailed effect prompt, whereas most baselines receive only the prompt. These results demonstrate the usefulness of additional reference information but do not establish superiority over methods designed for reference-conditioned video generation or suitable adaptation/personalization baselines.

The evaluation lacks ground-truth transferred videos. Reference embedding similarity can reward copying reference content rather than transferring only its effect, while input similarity rewards under-editing. No metric explicitly measures disentanglement of effect, reference identity/content, and target motion.

The paper does not provide a decisive diagnostic showing that RefVFX follows instance-specific temporal properties rather than recognizing an effect category from correlated reference and text cues. Tests with identical prompts but systematically varied reference timing, direction, intensity, or content, including mismatched-reference controls, would substantially strengthen the central claim.

The human-study reporting is insufficiently precise. It is unclear how many independent ratings each video pair receives, how trials are distributed among the 30 HITs per experiment, and what the effective sample size is. Standard deviations are reported rather than confidence intervals or hypothesis tests, yet statistical reliability is asserted without accounting for the many pairwise comparisons.

Several quantitative gains are modest: I2V reference similarity improves from 0.7230 to 0.7378 while first-frame similarity decreases, and general VBench statistics are mostly comparable or sometimes worse. Consequently, the scientific case relies heavily on subjective evaluation and selected qualitative examples.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a 14B-parameter LoRA fine-tuning effort: LoRA rank and target layers, optimizer, learning rate schedule, dropout probabilities, dataset mixture sizes, filtering criteria, and inference guidance weights are not fully specified. Code is promised, but release and licensing of the constructed dataset are unclear.

The dataset is dominated by human-centric and synthetic/generated content, and the 1,500 programmatic effects arise largely from combinations of a relatively small library of spatial filters and transitions. Thus, counts of distinct effects may overstate semantic diversity and broad real-world generalization.
Potential consent, licensing, bias, and misuse concerns associated with scraped public LoRAs, repurposed human videos, and realistic identity/body transformations are not meaningfully addressed.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and underexplored task: transferring a time-varying visual effect from a reference video while preserving a separate input video's content and motion. Reference-video conditioning is more expressive than text or static keyframes for this purpose.

The proposed training corpus is substantial in scale, combining LoRA-derived effects, a neural video-to-video generation pipeline, and reproducible programmatic effects into more than 120K triplets and 1,700 effect configurations.

The conditioning design is conceptually simple and practical, extending a strong Wan2.1 backbone without per-effect inference-time optimization. Separate classifier-free guidance directions also provide a useful trade-off between input preservation and reference adherence.

Evaluation includes I2V, neural V2V, and code-based V2V settings, an ablation without reference conditioning, several baselines, and a reasonably large human study. Reported overall-match preferences consistently favor RefVFX, generally by 60–67%.
The paper is visually clear and acknowledges limitations involving occlusion, complex interactions, human-centric training data, and approximately doubled inference cost.
weaknesses: The principal comparison is not well matched to the central claim. All external baselines are text-conditioned and cannot consume the reference video, so their weaker reproduction of fine-grained reference dynamics is largely expected. The No-Ref ablation helps establish that reference conditioning matters, but does not determine whether the proposed conditioning mechanism is better than straightforward reference-video alternatives. Adapted video style-transfer, motion-transfer, retrieval, or reference-attention baselines are needed.

The quantitative metrics do not isolate effect transfer. VideoPrism similarity between output and reference is strongly affected by subjects, backgrounds, appearance, and gross motion, although reference and target are intentionally content-mismatched. Likewise, input similarity rewards under-editing. The small differences in Table 3, such as 0.7378 versus 0.7230 reference similarity, therefore do not convincingly validate temporal-effect adherence.

The claimed generalization is inadequately characterized. The code-based evaluation holds out hyperparameter values while retaining the same hand-coded operators and transition families, which tests interpolation within templates rather than unseen effects. The neural validation set is manually filtered, contains only "over 100" instances, and lacks exact counts, category distributions, split construction, or tests on genuinely out-of-domain scenes and long-form effects.

The human-study evidence is incomplete despite being the strongest result. The paper gives aggregate win rates and bootstrap standard deviations but not the number of evaluated clips or judgments for each cell, confidence intervals or hypothesis tests, exclusion criteria, worker demographics, compensation, or inter-annotator agreement. Thirty HITs per experiment is modest, and the resampling unit and repeated-trial structure are not described precisely enough to assess independence.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a 14B-parameter training result. Important details such as LoRA rank and target modules, optimizer, learning rate and schedule, conditioning-dropout probabilities, sampling ratios within sources, neural-V2V dataset size, prompt lists, filtering criteria, and exact train/test splits are absent. Code is only promised after publication, while much of the dataset depends on third-party LoRAs and generated assets whose licenses and redistribution status are not discussed.

The manuscript calls the collection a new benchmark, yet supplies no ground-truth outputs for its validation pairs, no task-specific automatic metric, and no sufficiently specified evaluation protocol. It is better supported as a training dataset and preliminary evaluation set than as an established benchmark.

Most evidence for a fundamentally temporal task is presented as sparse frame strips. The manuscript points to an accompanying website for extensive videos, but the PDF contains only a placeholder link ("at this URL"). Without accessible videos, temporal coherence, timing correspondence, and failure frequency cannot be independently assessed from the submitted material.

The architecture contribution is modest and ambiguously documented: reference latents are largely concatenated spatially into an existing backbone, while the discussion of spatial versus channel concatenation and repeated reference information is difficult to reconcile. There are no architectural ablations comparing this design with cross-attention, separate reference encoders, or simpler concatenation strategies.

The method is restricted to 33 frames at 15 fps, roughly 2.2 seconds, and requires about seven minutes per 480p sample on an A100. There is no evaluation of longer sequences, effect timing under different input/reference durations, resolution scaling, or reference effects whose motion should not be copied literally.

Overall, the task and dataset idea have merit, but the unmatched baselines, confounded metrics, limited split analysis, and missing reproducibility details leave the central claims of faithful, generalizable temporal-effect transfer insufficiently established for acceptance.

strengths: The paper introduces a compelling and practically useful task: feed-forward transfer of time-varying visual effects from a reference video to a different image or video. This fills a meaningful gap between text-guided editing, static-reference conditioning, and per-effect optimization.

RefVFX combines a simple, well-motivated conditioning design with a substantial data contribution: more than 120K triplets spanning over 1,700 effects, assembled from complementary LoRA-based, generated video-to-video, and programmatic sources.

The data-generation pipeline is thoughtfully designed to produce motion-aligned input/output pairs, while the triplet construction encourages the model to separate an effect from the particular content of its reference video.

The evaluation covers image-to-video, neural video-to-video, and programmatic effects, with held-out effects and prompts. The qualitative examples show convincing transfer of transformations and temporal patterns that prompt-only baselines fail to reproduce.

The human study is unusually substantial, comprising more than 15,000 annotations from over 500 annotators. RefVFX is consistently preferred for overall match, typically by approximately 60–67%, and direct comparison to the no-reference ablation supports the value of reference conditioning.
The method provides useful inference-time control over the tradeoff between input preservation and reference-effect adherence through separate classifier-free guidance directions.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective, supplies extensive implementation and dataset details, and candidly discusses failures involving occlusion, interaction, domain concentration, and doubled inference cost.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are inherently asymmetric: RefVFX receives the full reference video whereas most baselines receive only a textual description. This demonstrates the value of the proposed task interface but does not cleanly isolate architectural superiority. The no-reference ablation helps, but comparisons to stronger generic video-reference conditioning or adaptation approaches would make the case more conclusive.

The validation set is relatively small—described only as over 100 instances—and partly produced using variants of the authors' own generation pipelines. Generalization to independently collected, natural reference videos and broader non-human scenes is therefore not established strongly.

The quantitative reference-similarity metric can reward copying the reference video's subjects, appearance, or scene rather than transferring only its effect. Conversely, input similarity may reward under-editing. These metrics are useful proxies but do not directly measure effect/content disentanglement.

Several important ablations are missing, including separate contributions of the three training-data sources, dataset scale and diversity, the width-wise reference-token design, text conditioning, and alternative reference-injection mechanisms. Consequently, it is difficult to determine which components drive the gains.

The user-study reporting could be more rigorous: exact numbers of evaluated items and judgments for each comparison are not given, bootstrap standard deviations are reported instead of confidence intervals, and significance or multiple-comparison treatment is not presented. Some preference margins, especially input-video adherence, are modest.

The dataset and reproducibility story remains incomplete. Code is promised upon publication, but release of the 120K triplets, complete LoRA provenance/licenses, generation prompts, filtering criteria, and all preprocessing scripts is not clearly committed to; training also requires eight A100 GPUs and inference takes about seven minutes per 33-frame video.

The method is demonstrated mainly on short, 33-frame, 480p, human-centric clips, with roughly twice the tokens and generation time of the base model. Robustness to longer sequences, arbitrary resolutions, large camera motion, environmental effects, and complex occlusions remains uncertain.
